One finding is recorded that applies beyond this compound: the monograph's rare-adverse-reaction list is word-for-word identical to the one printed in the DSIP monograph of the same handbook, which means it is boilerplate rather than a compound-specific observation.

compound.shortDescription: A peptide of the KISS1 gene family, first identified as a metastasis suppressor and used by practitioner sources for reproductive and gonadal support. No study of it is held here.
compound.simpleSummary:
Kisspeptin is a signalling peptide that sits near the top of the chain controlling reproductive hormones. It was first found in 1996 as something that suppressed the spread of melanoma cells, which is why its other name is metastin.

**The handbook lists a wide range of reproductive uses** — low testosterone, fertility, ovulation and implantation, hormone replacement — as well as insulin resistance, cancer and mood.

**This index holds no study of it.** Everything on this page is that one handbook.

**One of the listed uses deserves particular caution.** The handbook lists preventing ectopic pregnancy. That is a serious obstetric claim, and nothing held here supports it.

**The list of rare side effects is not specific to this compound.** The same four reactions appear word for word in another monograph of the same book, so they should be read as general boilerplate rather than as things observed with kisspeptin.
compound.practitionerSummary:
Kisspeptin is described by LaValle et al. as a gonadal axis support peptide, a 54-residue sequence of molecular weight 5857, other name metastin, derived from the KISS1 gene and first described in 1996 as a metastasis inhibitor in melanoma cell lines.

**The indication list spans reproductive endocrinology and more.** Primary hypogonadism, endogenous testosterone support, fertility support, improving ovulation and egg implantation, preventing ectopic pregnancy, physiologic hormone replacement, physiologic gonadotropin release, diabetes and insulin-resistance support, potential adjunct for metastatic prevention in cancer, and potential support for mood disorders.

**The regimen is 100 mcg subcutaneously daily at bedtime, five days a week**, supplied as 1 mg/ml in a 3 ml vial, with the source stating bedtime use is not required.

**Two limitations belong in a practitioner's reading of this record.** First, nothing held here supports any listed indication, and several of them — preventing ectopic pregnancy in particular — are consequential obstetric claims. Second, the monograph's rare-adverse-reaction list is identical to the one printed for DSIP in the same handbook, so it carries no compound-specific information.

**Kisspeptin-10 is not addressed by the source.** The sequence printed is the longer form; this index has not created an alias for the shorter fragment because the handbook does not mention it.
compound.unknownsSummary:
**No study of kisspeptin is held by this index** — for fertility, hypogonadism, ovulation, ectopic pregnancy, insulin resistance, cancer or mood. Every indication rests on one practitioner handbook.

**Preventing ectopic pregnancy is listed without any supporting evidence held here.** It is recorded because the source states it, and flagged because a reader encountering it should know that nothing in this index supports it.

**The rare-adverse-reaction list is boilerplate.** Erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia with hand oedema and rash appear verbatim in this handbook's DSIP monograph as well. Whatever those reactions describe, it is not something specific to kisspeptin, and this index does not present them as such.

**The relationship to kisspeptin-10 is unaddressed.** The monograph prints the longer sequence and does not discuss shorter fragments, which are what much of the research literature uses. Whether findings transfer between them is not established here.

**No literature screen has been run for kisspeptin.**

aliases.note: Listed by the handbook as another name, reflecting its first description as a metastasis inhibitor.

compound.molecularDescription: A 54-residue C-terminally amidated peptide of the KISS1 family, molecular weight 5857 g/mol as printed by the handbook. The held copy's rendering of the full sequence is long and partly garbled and has not been transcribed.
compound.nomenclatureNote: Kisspeptin names a family of peptides derived from the KISS1 gene by differential proteolysis, as the handbook itself states. The monograph prints the longer form and does not address kisspeptin-10 or other shorter fragments, so no alias has been created for them.

claims.claimText: LaValle et al. describe kisspeptin as a gonadal axis support peptide derived from the KISS1 gene, first discovered in 1996 as a metastasis inhibitor in melanoma cell lines, and state that kisspeptin is a family of structurally similar peptides formed by differential proteolysis.
claims.plainLanguageText: Kisspeptin comes from a gene called KISS1 and was first found as something that stopped melanoma cells spreading. It is a family of related peptides rather than a single one.
claims.interpretationNotes: The family point is the source's own and matters: it means a name alone does not identify which peptide is being discussed.
claims.uncertaintyText: The monograph prints one sequence and does not say which family member its regimen refers to, nor address the shorter fragments used in much of the research literature.
